The book of Acts is the second volume of ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧'s work, and it begins where his gospel ends. Once again it is addressed to ⟦p:theophilus_2849|Theophilus⟧. Once again the setting is ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, with a small group of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' followers waiting, as he told them to, for power from on high. From that room the story runs outward for some thirty years, from the early thirties of the first century to the early sixties, and from the temple courts of Jerusalem to a rented house in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧.

The traditional title, the Acts of the Apostles, was added later, and it promises more than the book sets out to give. Most of the Twelve are hardly mentioned after the opening chapters. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ follows two men above all, ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ in the first half of the book and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ in the second, and behind both of them the Holy Spirit, who drives the story on at every turn. The writer steps into his own story at intervals. In several passages, beginning in chapter sixteen, the narrative changes from they to we, and Luke is on the road with Paul. Those passages include the long voyage to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ at the end of the book.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' last words to his disciples, near the start of chapter one, give the book its map. You will be my witnesses in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and in all ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, and to the ends of the earth. The first seven chapters stay in Jerusalem. The coming of ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ at Pentecost, the first preaching, the life of the first community and the growing opposition of the temple authorities lead to the death of ⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧, the first to die for his faith in Jesus. In chapters eight to twelve the believers are scattered by persecution, and the message moves out into Judea and Samaria and beyond. ⟦p:philip_2347|Philip⟧ preaches to Samaritans and to an Ethiopian official. ⟦p:paul_2479|Saul of Tarsus⟧, a fierce persecutor, is stopped on the road to ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧. ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ is sent to the house of a Roman centurion in ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧, and Gentiles receive the Spirit. In ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧, the great city of ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧, a mixed congregation of Jews and Gentiles grows up, and there the disciples are first called Christians.

From chapter thirteen the story belongs to ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧, now known by his Roman name, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧. The church at ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧ sends him out with ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧, and ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ follows him on three great journeys. The first takes them to ⟦l:cyprus_316|Cyprus⟧ and to the towns of southern ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ Minor, in what is now Turkey. Then, in chapter fifteen, a council in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ settles whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧. On the second journey Paul and ⟦p:silas_2740|Silas⟧ cross the sea from Asia Minor into ⟦l:macedonia_747|Macedonia⟧, in northern ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧, and plant churches at ⟦l:philippi_942|Philippi⟧, ⟦l:thessalonica_1158|Thessalonica⟧ and ⟦l:berea_177|Berea⟧ before Paul moves on to ⟦l:athens_118|Athens⟧ and spends eighteen months at ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧. The third journey centres on ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧, where Paul stays some three years.

The world of these journeys is the Roman Empire at the height of its peace. Roman roads and shipping lanes tie it together, and Greek is spoken in every port. In almost every city there is a Jewish community with its synagogue, and often Gentiles who worship Israel's God without becoming Jews. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ usually begins there. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ names Roman officials with care, proconsuls, city magistrates and governors, each with his proper title. One of them, the proconsul ⟦p:gallio_1275|Gallio⟧, fixes Paul's time in ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧ in the early fifties.

Acts never mentions that ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ wrote letters, but many of them belong inside its story, and following Acts makes them easier to place. The letters to the Thessalonians were written from ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧, not long after Paul had been driven out of ⟦l:thessalonica_1158|Thessalonica⟧. The first letter to the Corinthians was written from ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧, the second from ⟦l:macedonia_747|Macedonia⟧, and Romans from Corinth, as Paul prepared to carry a gift of money to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. Galatians fights the same battle that the council of chapter fifteen settles. Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and ⟦p:philemon_2342|Philemon⟧ were written in prison in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧.

The last quarter of the book slows down. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ goes up to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ knowing that trouble awaits him, and he is seized in the temple courts and rescued from the mob by Roman soldiers. Two years of custody follow at ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧, the Roman capital of ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, where he defends himself before the governors ⟦p:felix_1257|Felix⟧ and ⟦p:portius_2367|Festus⟧ and before King ⟦p:agrippa_111|Agrippa⟧. Appealing to Caesar, he is sent to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ by sea, and ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧'s account of the voyage and the shipwreck off ⟦l:melita_761|Malta⟧ is one of the most vivid descriptions of ancient seafaring to survive.

Acts ends with ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ under house arrest for two years, receiving visitors and preaching openly. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ does not say how his trial ended. Both ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ and Paul died in Rome in the sixties, in the reign of Nero, but that lies beyond the book.

In the New Testament, Acts stands between the gospels and the letters, and it joins them. It tells how a movement that began among the Jewish followers of a crucified teacher from ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ came, within a single generation, to be found in the great cities of the empire, among Jews and Gentiles alike.
1:
⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ begins his second volume as he began the first, with a word to ⟦p:theophilus_2849|Theophilus⟧. He reminds him that the gospel told what ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ began to do and to teach, and he fills in what happened after the resurrection. For forty days Jesus appeared to the apostles and spoke with them about the kingdom of God. He told them not to leave ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, but to wait for the Holy Spirit the Father had promised.

The apostles still have one question on their minds: will he now restore the kingdom to Israel? ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' answer turns them outward, and it sketches the course of the whole book, from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ to ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ and to the ends of the earth. Then, on the Mount of Olives, he is taken up from their sight.

The rest of the chapter takes place in the days of waiting. The eleven apostles are named, and with them in the upper room are the women, ⟦p:mary_1938|Mary⟧ the mother of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, and his brothers, who, ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧'s gospel tells us, had not believed in him during his ministry. About a hundred and twenty believers are gathered when ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ stands up to speak about the place left empty by ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas⟧.
2:
About ten days after ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ was taken up, the believers are together in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ on the day of Pentecost. This was the Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival that fell fifty days after Passover, and one of the occasions when Jews came on pilgrimage to the city from far and wide.

When ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ comes, with a sound like a rushing wind and what look like tongues of fire, the believers begin to speak in other languages, and the crowd that gathers includes Jews from all over the known world. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧'s list sweeps from Parthia, beyond the eastern edge of the Roman Empire, through ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Mesopotamia⟧ and ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ Minor, to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, ⟦l:libya_730|Libya⟧, ⟦l:crete_310|Crete⟧, ⟦l:arabia_80|Arabia⟧ and ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ itself. Each one hears the wonders of God in his own language.

Then ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ stands up with the other apostles and gives the first sermon of the church. A few weeks earlier he had denied knowing ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ in a high priest's courtyard. Now he speaks to the crowds of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ about the man they crucified, drawing on the prophet ⟦p:joel_1660|Joel⟧ and on the Psalms of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧. The chapter ends with a portrait of the community that forms in the days that follow.
3:
The believers are still meeting daily in the temple courts. Now ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ tells one story from those days. ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ are going up to the temple for the afternoon prayer, at the ninth hour, about three o'clock. At the gate called Beautiful, one of the gates leading into the inner courts, sits a man who has been lame from birth, carried there every day to beg from the worshippers.

⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ appear together often in these early chapters. They had been partners in the fishing business on the Sea of ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, and they were among the three closest to ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. Now they are leaders in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.

What happens at the gate draws a large crowd to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s Colonnade, a long covered walkway along the eastern side of the temple's outer court. ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ seizes the moment to speak again. In this second sermon he tells the people of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ plainly that they handed ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ over to ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧ and asked for a murderer instead. He calls them to repentance, and he grounds his appeal in ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, in the prophets from ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ onwards, and in the promise made to ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧.
4:
⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ is still speaking in ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s Colonnade when the temple authorities arrive: priests, the captain of the temple guard, and members of the Sadducees, the party of the high priestly families. They are disturbed above all that the apostles are proclaiming resurrection from the dead through ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. Peter and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ are held overnight, and yet the number of believing men grows to about five thousand.

The next morning they stand before the council, the Sanhedrin, and ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ names the men facing them: ⟦p:annas_269|Annas⟧, ⟦p:caiaphas_532|Caiaphas⟧ and others of the high priest's family. These are the same leaders who handed ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ over to ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧ only weeks before. The council members notice that ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ are ordinary men without formal training in the law, and they recognise them as men who had been with Jesus.

After their release, the two return to the believers, who pray together in the words of the second Psalm about rulers raging against the Lord's anointed. The chapter closes with a picture of a community sharing its possessions, and with a man who will be important later: ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧, a Levite from the island of ⟦l:cyprus_316|Cyprus⟧, whom the apostles call ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧, meaning son of encouragement.
5:
⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ has just sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. The chapter opens with a couple who do the same, or appear to. ⟦p:ananias_258|Ananias⟧ and his wife ⟦p:sapphira_2472|Sapphira⟧ sell a property and keep back part of the money while pretending to give it all. What follows is a sobering moment in the life of the young community.

The apostles' healing work draws the sick from the towns around ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and the high priest and his circle, all Sadducees, are filled with jealousy. They arrest the apostles and put them in the public jail, but the next morning the prisoners are found teaching in the temple courts again.

Brought before the Sanhedrin once more, the apostles refuse to be silent. The council is ready to have them killed when a respected Pharisee named ⟦p:gamaliel_1277|Gamaliel⟧, one of the most honoured teachers of the law in his day, rises to counsel caution. He reminds them of other movements that rose and collapsed when their leaders died. Years later, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ will say that he was educated at Gamaliel's feet. The apostles are flogged and released, and they go out rejoicing.
6:
The believers in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ are growing fast, and growth brings strain. The community now includes two groups of Jews. The Hebraic Jews were local, at home in Aramaic and the ways of the land. The Grecian Jews had come from the cities of the dispersion, spoke Greek as their first language, and many had settled in Jerusalem. When the Grecian widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food, the complaint reaches the apostles.

The answer is to appoint seven men to oversee the work. All seven have Greek names, and one, Nicolas, is a convert from ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧. Two of them will matter greatly in the chapters ahead. One is ⟦p:philip_2347|Philip⟧, not the apostle of that name but a different man. The other is ⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧, full of faith and of the Holy Spirit.

⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧'s preaching soon brings him into conflict with members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen, descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, with links to ⟦l:cyrene_317|Cyrene⟧, ⟦l:alexandria_46|Alexandria⟧, ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ and ⟦l:cilicia_300|Cilicia⟧, the province that included ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧'s home city of ⟦l:tarsus_1140|Tarsus⟧. They bring him before the Sanhedrin with charges that echo those once brought against ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧: that he speaks against the temple and the law.
7:
⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧ stands before the Sanhedrin, accused of speaking against the temple and the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧. The high priest asks him whether the charges are true. What follows is the longest speech in Acts.

⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧ does not answer directly. Instead he retells the story of Israel, from God's call to ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ in ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Mesopotamia⟧, through ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧ in ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ and ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ in the wilderness, to the tabernacle and the temple built by ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧. Listeners who know Genesis and Exodus will recognise every step, but Stephen chooses his emphases with care. God appears to Abraham far from the promised land, and he is with Joseph in Egypt and with Moses at a burning bush in the desert. And again and again Israel turns against the deliverers God sends, first Joseph, then Moses. The speech builds toward the temple, and toward the claim that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands.

At the end ⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧ turns on his judges directly, and the hearing becomes a riot. He is dragged outside the city and stoned. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ adds a quiet detail: the witnesses lay their cloaks at the feet of a young man named ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧.
8:
⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧ is dead, and the young man named ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ approved of his killing. For now ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ shows him as the leading persecutor of the church, going from house to house and dragging believers off to prison. Persecution breaks out against the believers in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and all but the apostles are scattered through ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. Those who scatter take the message with them.

⟦p:philip_2347|Philip⟧, another of the seven chosen in chapter six, goes north to a city in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. Jews and Samaritans had long kept apart, yet the Samaritans welcome his message. Among those who believe is a man named ⟦p:simon_2752|Simon⟧, who has amazed the city with his sorcery, and whose name later gave the word simony to the buying of spiritual office. The apostles in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ send ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧, and they pray for the Samaritans to receive the Holy Spirit.

Then ⟦p:philip_2347|Philip⟧ is sent south to the desert road that runs from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ toward ⟦l:gaza_446|Gaza⟧. There he meets a court official from the kingdom ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ calls Ethiopia, the ancient land of Cush on the upper ⟦l:nile_895|Nile⟧, in what is now Sudan. He is treasurer to the queen, known by the title Candace, and he is riding home in his chariot, reading the prophet ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ aloud.
9:
⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧, the young man at whose feet the witnesses laid their cloaks when ⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧ was stoned, is still breathing out threats against the Lord's disciples. Born in ⟦l:tarsus_1140|Tarsus⟧ in ⟦l:cilicia_300|Cilicia⟧ and educated in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ as a Pharisee, he now asks the high priest for letters to arrest followers of the Way, as the movement was then called, in the synagogues of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, some hundred and fifty miles to the north-east.

He never arrives as he intended. Near the city a light from heaven flashes around him, a voice speaks his name, and ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ is led into ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ by the hand, blind. Acts will tell this story twice more, in ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s own defence speeches. For three days he neither eats nor drinks, until a disciple of the city named ⟦p:ananias_259|Ananias⟧, not the man of chapter five, is sent to him at a house on Straight Street. Saul soon begins preaching in the synagogues, until a plot forces him to escape over the city wall. In his letter to the Galatians Paul adds that he spent time in ⟦l:arabia_80|Arabia⟧, and that three years passed before he went up to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. There ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ vouches for him, before threats send him home to ⟦l:tarsus_1140|Tarsus⟧.

Then ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ turns back to ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧, travelling in the coastal plain, at ⟦l:lydda_741|Lydda⟧ and at ⟦l:joppa_652|Joppa⟧, the old seaport of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. He lodges with a tanner named ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧, a trade many Jews avoided because it meant handling dead animals.
10:
⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ is staying in ⟦l:joppa_652|Joppa⟧, in the house of ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧ the tanner by the sea. About thirty miles up the coast lies ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧, a splendid port built by ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ the Great and now the seat of the Roman governors of ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧.

In ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧ lives ⟦p:cornelius_956|Cornelius⟧, a centurion of the unit known as the Italian Regiment. He is a Gentile, but he is one of those ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ calls God-fearing, a man who worships Israel's God, prays regularly and gives generously, without having become a Jew. An angel tells him to send for ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧.

The next day, at noon, ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ goes up on the flat roof of the tanner's house to pray. He is hungry, and he falls into a trance in which he sees a great sheet let down from heaven, full of animals the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ forbade Jews to eat. Many Jews kept strictly apart from Gentiles, and a devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile's house or share his table. When ⟦p:cornelius_956|Cornelius⟧' messengers arrive at the gate, Peter has to decide whether to go with them, and what he finds waiting in ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧ will change the church for good.
11:
By the time ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ returns to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, the believers there have heard that Gentiles in ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧ have received the word of God, and some of the Jewish believers are troubled that Peter entered a Gentile house and ate with uncircumcised men. Peter tells the story again from the beginning, and the matter is settled, at least for now.

Then ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ turns north. Some of those scattered after ⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧'s death have reached ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧, on the Orontes river in ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧, one of the largest cities of the Roman world. There, men from ⟦l:cyprus_316|Cyprus⟧ and ⟦l:cyrene_317|Cyrene⟧ begin speaking about ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ not only to Jews but to Greeks, and many believe. It is the first church we hear of where large numbers of Gentiles and Jews belong together.

The ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ church sends ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ to see what is happening, and Barnabas goes on to ⟦l:tarsus_1140|Tarsus⟧ to find ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧. The two spend a full year teaching in ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧, and it is there that the disciples are first called Christians. The chapter ends with a prophet named ⟦p:agabus_107|Agabus⟧ predicting a famine, which came in the reign of the emperor ⟦p:claudius_947|Claudius⟧, and with Barnabas and Saul carrying relief to the believers in ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧.
12:
While ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ and ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ are carrying famine relief to ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ turns back to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. The king there is ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ ⟦p:agrippa_111|Agrippa⟧ the First, a grandson of Herod the Great, who had grown up partly in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ among the imperial family and now ruled Judea by the favour of the emperor Claudius.

⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ has ⟦p:james_717|James⟧, the brother of ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧, put to death with the sword, the first of the Twelve to die for his faith. Seeing that this pleases the people, he arrests ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ too, at the time of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and means to bring him out before the people once the Passover is over. On the night before his trial Peter lies asleep between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with guards at the door, while the church prays for him.

Two new names appear in this chapter. ⟦p:mary_1941|Mary⟧, in whose house the believers are praying, is the mother of ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧, also called ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧, who will soon travel with ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ and ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ and will one day write the second gospel. And ⟦p:james_717|James⟧, to whom ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ sends word, is the brother of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, now a leader of the church in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.

The chapter ends in ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧ with ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧'s sudden death, in the year forty-four. Then ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ and ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ return to ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧, bringing ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ with them.
13:

16:

17:

18:

19:

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ stays here longer than anywhere else on his travels, some three years in all. 20:

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has been rescued from the mob in the temple courts and carried up the steps toward the Roman barracks, in the Antonia fortress that overlooked the temple from the north-west. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ stands before the Sanhedrin, with the Roman commander looking on. 24:
Five days after ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s arrival in ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧, his accusers come down from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧: the high priest ⟦p:ananias_260|Ananias⟧, some elders, and a professional advocate named ⟦p:tertullus_2844|Tertullus⟧, who will present their case in the proper Roman manner. ⟦p:portius_2367|Porcius Festus⟧ has just taken office as governor of ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, and he inherits ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s case, unresolved after two years. ⟦p:portius_2367|Festus⟧ hears the case at ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧ instead, but when he asks whether ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ is willing to be tried in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, Paul invokes his right as a Roman citizen to have his case heard by the emperor himself. Before ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ can be sent, there are visitors. King ⟦p:agrippa_111|Agrippa⟧, ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ Agrippa the Second, is the son of the Herod who died in chapter twelve and the last of the Herodian kings. 26:
The next day, in the audience hall at ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧, the whole of local high society has gathered: King ⟦p:agrippa_111|Agrippa⟧ and ⟦p:bernice_482|Bernice⟧ in their finery, the governor ⟦p:portius_2367|Festus⟧, the military commanders and the leading men of the city. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ is brought in, still in chains, and Agrippa gives him permission to speak.

27:
The decision has been made to send ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ by sea. 28:
The ship has broken up on a sandbar, but everyone on board has reached the shore alive, on the island of ⟦l:melita_761|Malta⟧, south of Sicily.
